passages.title: KINDNESS WEEK CAMPAIGN
passages.content: The Student Council is delighted to launch “Kindness Week”, a series of activities designed to spread positivity throughout our school community. If every student (1) ______ part in at least one kind act each day, our school will feel warmer and friendlier by the end of the week. Our main objective is to raise students’ (2) ______ of the value of small, everyday gestures. To support this, kindness boxes will be (3) ______ near every classroom for students to drop in anonymous notes of appreciation. Peer-support workshops will also be organised to help students come (4) ______ with practical ways to comfort a struggling classmate. These sessions are designed to make compassion a habit rather than a one-off occasion. We hope to (5) ______ a culture of empathy that lasts well beyond this single week. We firmly believe that small daily gestures will accumulate into something far greater over time. Teachers will be on hand to support students throughout the week’s activities. Please register your class’s planned activities with the Student Council office. Your (6) ______ is essential to the success of this campaign. Don’t hesitate – join the wave of kindness today!

Among the many quirks of human perception, one deserves particular attention: the conviction that everyone around us is watching our every move. Psychologists refer to this tendency as the spotlight effect, a bias (12) ______. Imagine tripping in a crowded hallway or wearing a shirt with an unfortunate stain; the assumption that this small mishap will be remembered by everyone who witnessed it is, more often than not, wildly overstated.

Experiments repeatedly reveal a striking gap between how conspicuous we feel and how much others actually register. Participants (13) ______ consistently overestimated how many people in the room would later recall their T-shirt. (14) ______.

This matters because the spotlight effect quietly fuels social anxiety, (15) ______ – a presentation, a first date, an awkward silence – long after everyone else has forgotten it. (16) ______. Recognising the bias for what it is offers a small but genuine form of relief: most of the audience, it seems, was never really watching.

Few industries have expanded as rapidly over the past two decades as fast fashion, a business model built on churning out inexpensive, trend-driven clothing at a punishing pace. A t-shirt that costs less than a cup of coffee might appear to be an unambiguous bargain, yet very little about that garment’s price reflects what it genuinely costs to produce. Whenever a price fails to capture the full expense of making something, someone else, somewhere else, ends up settling the difference.

The environmental side of that unpaid bill is considerable. Producing a single cotton t-shirt can require several thousand litres of water, much of it drawn from regions already facing scarcity. Dyeing and finishing processes discharge chemical run-off into rivers that supply drinking water to nearby communities. Meanwhile, garments designed to be discarded after a handful of wears accumulate in landfills at a rate that recycling infrastructure has never come close to matching.

[I] The human cost is no less severe, even though it rarely appears on a price tag. [II] Many garment workers earn wages that fall well below what is needed to cover basic living expenses in the cities where their factories are located. [III] Extended shifts in poorly ventilated facilities, combined with exposure to dust and chemical fumes, have also been linked to chronic respiratory conditions among factory workers. [IV] Brands are rarely required to disclose any of these conditions, leaving consumers with little means of judging what a garment truly cost to make.

None of this means fast fashion cannot be reformed, but doing so requires abandoning the fiction that a five-dollar garment is somehow cost-free to produce. Economists sometimes refer to this gap as an externality: a cost generated by one party but shifted onto another, whether that be a river downstream, a worker’s lungs, or a landfill’s dwindling capacity. Until such costs are reflected somewhere in the price we pay, the true bill for fast fashion will simply continue to be paid by those least able to afford it.

passages.title: CAMPUS RADIO PRESENTER WANTED
passages.content: Wave FM, our university’s student-run radio station, is looking for two enthusiastic presenters to join the team this term. The more confident you sound behind the microphone, the (27) ______ likely you are to be shortlisted for an audition. Successful candidates will gain valuable broadcasting experience, a modest stipend, and access to industry contacts. (28) ______, we offer a flexible schedule that can be arranged around lecture timetables. On top of that, (29) ______ prior broadcasting experience is required, as full training is provided to every new presenter. If you (30) ______ any questions about the role, feel free to drop by the station office before Friday. Applications should be submitted by email to wavefm@campus.edu no later than 25 October. Rarely has there been such a(n) (31) ______ opportunity to gain hands-on media experience while still a student. (32) ______ miss out – tune in and apply today!

Ask most students how they prepare for an exam and the answer usually involves rereading a textbook chapter or highlighting a stack of notes in vivid colour. Such methods feel productive, largely because the material grows increasingly familiar with each pass. That sense of familiarity, however, is a notoriously unreliable guide to how well the information has actually been learned.

Cognitive scientists have spent decades comparing rereading against a rival strategy known as retrieval practice, or simply, self-testing. In one now-classic study, students who studied a passage once and then quizzed themselves repeatedly on its content outperformed students who reread the same passage four times, despite having spent far less total time with the material. The advantage held up not only immediately afterwards but, more strikingly, a week later.

Researchers attribute this to what they call desirable difficulty: the mental effort of pulling information out of memory, rather than simply recognising it on a page, appears to strengthen the very connections that make recall possible later on. Retrieval only helps, though, when learners can check their answers and correct their mistakes; without that feedback loop, students risk rehearsing errors as confidently as they rehearse facts.

None of this means rereading is entirely useless, particularly during a first encounter with unfamiliar material. Nor is self-testing a magic formula on its own: cramming a single, marathon quiz session into the night before an exam brings only a fraction of the benefit that comes from spacing several shorter sessions across the preceding weeks. Once the basics are in place, students are better served by closing the book, asking themselves what they remember, checking their answers, and repeating the process a few days later rather than a few hours later. The discomfort of struggling to recall an answer, far from being a sign that studying has failed, is frequently the very mechanism through which durable learning occurs.
